title: What is time? (Confessions 11.14)
hookLine: if no one asks me, I know; if I try to explain, I don't
tomorrow: why would a strict monk's rulebook promise nothing harsh?

cards: A phone knows what time it is, to the second. Ask it what time is, and it hands back a definition that explains nothing. Augustine is at that exact spot, pen in hand, deep in the Confessions.
He has just been talking to God about the first line of Genesis, a beginning before any clock. Then he stops and asks it plainly: what, then, is time? Nothing, he says, do we talk about more easily.
Late, soon, yesterday, someday, a long while, a moment ago. So he tries to answer, and what comes out is a confession of a different kind.

teach.h: IF NO ONE ASKS ME, I KNOW.
teach.b: If no one asks me, I know. If I try to explain it to someone who asks, I don't. Then he works the puzzle out loud.

teach.h: THE PAST IS GONE; THE FUTURE ISN'T YET.
teach.b: The past isn't anymore. The future isn't yet. So only the present is.

teach.h: A PRESENT THAT STAYED WOULD BE ETERNITY.
teach.b: But if the present stayed present and never slid into the past, it wouldn't be time at all. It would be eternity. So the present only is, he says, because it's on its way to not being.

He isn't playing with words, and he isn't showing off. Book Eleven is reading Genesis, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth," and the God he's praying to doesn't live in passing time.
A little further on, Augustine finds where past and future actually live: in the mind, now.
A present of things past, which is memory. A present of things present, which is attention. A present of things future, which is expectation.
Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: in Augustine's picture, nobody ever visits yesterday or tomorrow. We only remember and hope, and both happen right now.
The carry gives that a short shape, though the text never turns it into a slogan. It leaves Augustine still asking God to help him understand, standing in the one moment that is.

how: Some Christians read Augustine's Confessions slowly, a few pages at a time, as a book of prayer as much as a book of ideas.

o: Augustine's question about what passing time really is
a riddle about the clocks monks kept for prayer
a question about managing a crowded schedule

games.q: what is time? — tap the pairs.

s: Augustine says time is just an illusion
the popular version. he says he knows it until asked, and finds past and future present in the mind.
Augustine says a present that never passed would be eternity
if the present stayed present, it wouldn't be time at all.
Augustine can explain time easily to anyone who asks
if no one asks, he knows; when he tries to explain, he doesn't.

games.q: at dinner, your grandpa keeps saying 'back in my day' and your sister keeps saying 'when i move out.' by Augustine, where are they both?
o: one is stuck in the past, one in the future; neither is here.
both are here: one remembering, one hoping, right now.
nowhere; only clocks really hold time.
games.why: for Augustine, the past lives now as memory and the future now as expectation. both of them are at the table.

practice: Listen for one sound in the room: a fan, traffic, your own breathing. Each time you catch it, it's already passing and already new. When your mind runs off to yesterday or later, call it memory or hope, and come back to the sound.

wordCard.voice: What is time? Augustine's question in Book Eleven: easy until someone asks, and only the passing present truly here.

orig.note: Latin: time. Augustine's question in Confessions 11.14 is quid est ergo tempus? what then is time?

carryVoice: Keep this: now is all we have, with the past held as memory and the future as hope. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
